reading.body:
AI's physical plant has become an insurance problem: ten distinct property exposures, from coolant leaks to drone strikes, now shape where compute gets built and what it costs to keep it covered.

The exposures cluster around what AI changed physically. Direct-to-chip cooling puts fluid inside the rack next to energised equipment, and liquid-related damage accounts for close to a quarter of data centre loss costs across fifteen years, per Swiss Re, which is why FM added a liquid-cooling section to its 2026 loss prevention guidance. Racks above 100 kW raise structural floor loading questions when legacy buildings are retrofitted. Sudden AI workload spikes overheat substations and transformers. Battery storage and small modular reactor co-location appear because campuses need power the grid cannot always supply, and water use and environmental impairment follow from cooling at scale. These are consequences of denser compute, not generic property risks.

For AI specifically, insurance acts as a gate on siting and operation, not just a cost line. Premium increases and refusals for campuses in fire or flood exposed regions, reinsurance maps that price seismic, coastal surge and grid vulnerability by geography, and sabotage exclusion wording that reaches any site near contested airspace all bear on where capacity can be financed and run. Drone strikes on three AWS facilities in the UAE and Bahrain in March 2026 moved geopolitical exclusion review from a theoretical underwriting question to a live one for Gulf-region operators.

What the data does not give is scale. There are no premiums, no claim totals beyond the Swiss Re share, no counts of affected sites, and no comparison across operators or regions. It is a taxonomy of exposure categories rather than a measurement of realised loss, and it does not say whether any project was cancelled, moved, or repriced as a result.

Loss correlation, not just loss frequency, is what changed. Direct-to-chip cooling places fluid inside the rack next to energised equipment, so a leak can damage the compute itself rather than only the building, and liquid-related damage already accounts for close to a quarter of data centre loss costs across fifteen years, per Swiss Re. FM's 2026 loss prevention guidance now treats liquid cooling as its own section, which means underwriters inspect for it as a distinct hazard.

The data supports a shift from location-only underwriting to design-and-operation underwriting. Racks above 100 kW raise structural floor loading questions when legacy buildings are retrofitted, continuous maximum load through extreme heat produces HVAC and chiller breakdown claims, and battery storage or small modular reactor co-location add fire, liability and framework questions that follow from needing power the grid cannot always supply. Reinsurers still price seismic, coastal surge and grid vulnerability by geography, but the new exposures are created by how the building is used, not only where it sits.

The practical consequence is that insurance terms now reach into engineering and siting decisions together. A campus in a fire or flood exposed region faces premium increases or refusals, while a site near contested airspace carries sabotage exclusion wording after drone strikes on three AWS facilities in the UAE and Bahrain in March 2026. Operators cannot separate the power decision from the property cover decision.

What does direct-to-chip liquid cooling do to data centre insurance?

Direct-to-chip cooling puts fluid inside the rack next to energised equipment. Liquid-related damage accounts for close to a quarter of data centre loss costs across fifteen years, per Swiss Re, and FM added a liquid-cooling section to its 2026 loss prevention guidance.

How do insurers treat data centres in wildfire or flood zones?

Insurers apply premium increases and refusals for campuses built in fire or flood exposed regions. The data does not give specific premium amounts or refusal rates.

What happened with drone strikes on AWS facilities?

Drone strikes hit three AWS facilities in the UAE and Bahrain in March 2026. This moved geopolitical exclusion review from a theoretical underwriting question to a live one for Gulf-region operators, and the same wording reaches any site near contested airspace.

Does the data show actual premiums or claim totals?

No. The data has no premiums, no claim totals beyond the Swiss Re share, no counts of affected sites, and no comparison across operators or regions. It is a taxonomy of exposure categories rather than a measurement of realised loss.

What is the insurance issue with racks above 100 kW?

Retrofitting legacy buildings for racks exceeding 100 kW raises structural floor loading questions. The data does not say whether any specific building was rejected or reinforced.

How do reinsurers price site selection?

Reinsurers price seismic, coastal surge and grid vulnerability by geography. The data does not give the actual maps or price differences.
